981.title: Udham Singh, 1940
981.hook: a survivor of Jallianwala shot the former Punjab governor in London and was hanged
981.howItsDone: Udham Singh is honored in Punjab as a shaheed; his memorials, his name on public places and his anniversary are kept there, and his story is told alongside the memory of Jallianwala Bagh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, siropa, and your line was outrage became reform. Did you speak up once about a wrong honor? Today, one man who carried Jallianwala Bagh for a very long time. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

London, 1940. A meeting hall in Westminster, full of officials and guests listening to speeches about India. Near the end, a man in the audience stands up, draws a revolver, and fires. Among those hit is Sir Michael O'Dwyer, who had been the lieutenant governor of Punjab when the troops fired at Jallianwala Bagh. O'Dwyer dies. The man with the gun is seized before he can leave the hall. His name is Udham Singh, and he has come a very long way, in miles and in years, to stand in that room.
screen: `A MEETING HALL IN LONDON.` → `A MAN STANDS AND FIRES.` → `HE IS SEIZED IN THE HALL.`

segments.voice: First, the memory. Udham Singh grew up in an orphanage in Amritsar. Sikh and Punjabi memory holds that he was at Jallianwala Bagh on the day of the firing, and that what he saw there never left him. Some historians question whether he was there, and the sources don't settle it. Either way, the lieutenant governor who had backed the general became, for him, the name of that day. Second, the years. He did not act quickly. He traveled, worked, was jailed, and eventually reached England. The shooting in London came long after the garden in Amritsar. That's today's line: a long memory. Third, the name. Accounts of his trial say that he gave his name as Ram Mohammad Singh Azad: a Hindu name, a Muslim name and a Sikh name together, and azad, which means free. He was tried, convicted and hanged in London. Fourth, how he's remembered. In Punjab he is honored as a shaheed, a martyr, and his ashes were later brought home. Others, then and since, have judged the killing differently, and the Sikh tradition itself teaches deep caution about anger. The name he chose points to something the Guru Granth Sahib says plainly. At Ang 1349, Bhagat Kabir sings that from one light the whole world came into being, so who can be called good and who bad? Whatever people conclude about his act, the name Udham Singh chose refused to divide the people of Punjab.

segments.voice: Two minutes with a long memory. Sit, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind something from long ago that you still carry: a hurt, a loss, a day that changed things. Don't replay it. Just notice that you're still holding it. Breathe in, and notice whatever weight it has today. Breathe out, and let your hands rest open. You're not asked to forget, or to forgive on the spot. Only to sit beside the memory without letting it steer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Udham Singh. The man who, years after Jallianwala Bagh, shot Punjab's former lieutenant governor in London, gave his name as Ram Mohammad Singh Azad, and was hanged. Today's word.
Your line: a long memory. Today, ask an older person what they remember that the rest of the family has forgotten, and just listen. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

982.title: Bhagat Singh
982.hook: born into a Sikh family, the young revolutionary later wrote of doubting God, and is honored across Punjab
982.howItsDone: Bhagat Singh is remembered across Punjab, by Sikhs and by others, as a shaheed of the freedom struggle; his picture hangs in homes and shops, and his anniversary is marked with gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udham Singh, and your line was a long memory. Did an older person tell you something the family had forgotten? Today, a young man whose face is painted on walls across Punjab. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

On a truck's back panel, on a college wall, on a sticker on a scooter: the same young face, a mustache, sometimes a turban, sometimes a hat tilted to one side. Ask the driver who it is and you'll get two words, said with real pride. Bhagat Singh. Ask what he believed about God, and the answer gets more interesting. He was born into a Sikh family. And near the end of his short life, in a prison cell, he sat down and wrote out, as carefully as he could, why he no longer believed.
screen: `THE SAME FACE ON TRUCKS AND WALLS.` → `TURBAN OR HAT.` → `A PRISON CELL, AND A PEN.`

segments.voice: First, the family. Bhagat Singh grew up in a Sikh household in Punjab, in a family already caught up in the struggle against British rule. Second, the revolutionary. As a young man he turned to armed struggle against the British, and that path ended in a trial in Lahore. He was hanged there, together with two companions, Sukhdev and Rajguru. Third, the essay. While waiting in prison, he wrote a piece titled Why I Am an Atheist. In it he explains, plainly and without mockery, how he came to doubt God, and he insists that he arrived there by thinking it through, not out of pride. He writes, too, that he expects to face the gallows without turning to belief for comfort at the end. Fourth, the honor. Bhagat Singh is honored across Punjab and beyond by religious and non-religious people alike. Some Sikhs who pray every morning keep his picture on the wall. Those who share his doubt claim him too. Nobody needs to settle his beliefs to honor his courage and his candor. And Guru Nanak gives the Sikh measure of a life, at Ang 62 of the Guru Granth Sahib: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Bhagat Singh's conclusions about God are his own, and Sikh teaching does not share them. What his admirers point to is that he didn't pretend. He said what he thought, and he lived it to the end. That's today's line.
screen: `A SIKH HOUSEHOLD IN PUNJAB.` · `ARMED STRUGGLE, A TRIAL, THE GALLOWS.` · `WHY I AM AN ATHEIST.` · `HIGHER STILL IS TRUTHFUL LIVING.` · then, large: `AN HONEST MIND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for an honest doubter. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone who doesn't believe what you believe, or who believes nothing at all, and who has told you so honestly. Picture their face as they said it. Notice any urge to argue, and let it pass on the next breath out. Then find one thing to respect in them: their honesty, their care, the way they thought it through. Hold that for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhagat Singh. A young revolutionary from a Sikh family, hanged in Lahore, who wrote in prison of why he doubted God, and is honored across Punjab. Today's word.
Your line: an honest mind. Today, when someone tells you plainly what they think, even if you disagree, thank them for saying it straight. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

983.title: The SGPC, 1920
983.hook: Sikhs formed a committee to manage gurdwaras and a volunteer band, the Akali Dal
983.howItsDone: The SGPC today manages historic gurdwaras in Punjab and neighboring regions, including the Golden Temple; Sikhs also do seva in gurdwaras everywhere as volunteers, in the kitchen, cleaning and looking after shoes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat Singh, and your line was an honest mind. Did you thank someone for saying it straight? Today, back to the gurdwaras, and the outrage over the robe turns into a plan. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

Four letters, printed on signboards and letterheads in Punjab: S, G, P, C. You can pass them without a second look. Behind them is a long name, the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, and behind the long name is a question Sikhs had been asking since the robe was given to the general. Who should look after the gurdwaras? In 1920, at a gathering in Amritsar, Sikhs gave their answer. We will. Today: the SGPC.
screen: `FOUR LETTERS ON SIGNBOARDS.` → `A LONG NAME BEHIND THEM.` → `WHO LOOKS AFTER THE GURDWARAS?`

segments.voice: First, the problem. Gurdwaras were then often in the hands of mahants, hereditary custodians, and some treated the shrines and their lands as private property. Some practices crept in that reformers said went against the Gurus' teaching, and at the Golden Temple the manager answered to the government. Second, the committee. In 1920 Sikhs met in Amritsar and formed a committee to take over the management of the gurdwaras on behalf of the Panth, the whole Sikh community. Its long name means, roughly, the chief committee for managing the gurdwaras. Third, the volunteers. Alongside it came a band of volunteers called the Akali Dal. Akali comes from Akal, the Timeless One, a name for God, and the volunteers were called Akalis. They were not paid soldiers. They were farmers, teachers, former servicemen and students who gave their time, and later their bodies, to the work. Fourth, why it's seva. Guru Nanak says, at Ang 26 of the Guru Granth Sahib, that if you serve in this world, you'll be given a seat in the court of the Lord. The reform movement was political, and the SGPC later became a powerful elected body. But at the start it ran on seva: ordinary people offering to do the job no one was paying them for. That's today's line.

segments.voice: Two minutes to choose one task. Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of the places you belong to: a home, a workplace, a street, a gurdwara, a club. In one of them, there's a job nobody wants. The dishes after the meal. The chairs after the meeting. The form no one fills in. Picture it clearly. Now picture yourself quietly doing it, with no one asking. Breathe slowly, and decide on one task you'll take on. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Your line: volunteers stepped up. Today, do the one task you chose, the one nobody asked you to do. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: Tarn Taran, 1921
984.hook: reformers were attacked seeking to take over the gurdwara
984.howItsDone: Sikhs visit the gurdwara at Tarn Taran, with its large sarovar, as a historic shrine; the reformers who died there are remembered among the martyrs of the gurdwara reform movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the SGPC, and your line was volunteers stepped up. Did you do the task nobody asked for? Today, the volunteers arrive at a gurdwara, and it goes badly. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

Early in 1921, a band of reformers walks into a town south of Amritsar, where a gurdwara stands beside a wide sacred pool. Tradition says Guru Arjan founded the town. They have come, singing, to ask the priests who hold the shrine to hand it over to the Panth. They talk, and they wait to be heard. Night falls. They're still there, waiting, when the priests' men come at them with weapons. Today: Tarn Taran.
screen: `A SACRED POOL SOUTH OF AMRITSAR.` → `REFORMERS COME TO TALK.` → `AT NIGHT, AN ATTACK.`

segments.voice: First, why they came. The custodians at Tarn Taran were accused by the reformers of allowing practices in the shrine that went against the Gurus' teaching, and of treating its offerings as their own. The reformers came to take over its management for the newly formed committee. Second, the attack. Accounts say that while they waited, the priests and the men with them attacked the reformers, who were struck with sticks and blades. Several were badly wounded, and some died of their wounds. Third, the response. The reformers did not answer the attack with an attack. They held their ground, cared for the wounded, and the shrine in the end passed to the Panth's management. Calm, here, did not mean quiet. It meant not letting someone else's violence choose your next move. Fourth, the Guru's line. Guru Tegh Bahadur, in a salok at Ang 1427 of the Guru Granth Sahib, praises the one who frightens no one and fears no one. Both halves matter. The reformers came without frightening anyone, and they didn't run when they were frightened. Tradition explains the name Tarn Taran as a boat that carries people across. That night, the people who came to the pool needed something to carry them through. They found it in staying still. That's today's line.

segments.voice: Two minutes to practice calm in conflict. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a recent argument, or a moment when someone came at you with sharp words. Notice whether your body reacts even now: the jaw, the shoulders, the chest. Breathe in slowly. On the breath out, let the jaw go. Again, and let the shoulders drop. This isn't giving in. It's refusing to let the other person's anger set your pace. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Tarn Taran. A gurdwara town south of Amritsar, where reformers who came to talk were attacked at night and held their ground. Today's word.
Your line: calm under attack. Today, the next time someone comes at you sharply, take one full breath before you answer. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: Nankana, the full story
985.hook: at Guru Nanak's birthplace in 1921 the mahant's men killed many peaceful reformers, including Bhai Lachhman Singh
985.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Nankana massacre as the Saka Nankana Sahib, with an annual remembrance in February; pilgrims to Gurdwara Janam Asthan bow at the jand tree associated with Bhai Lachhman Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tarn Taran, and your line was calm under attack. Did you take one full breath before answering someone sharp? Today, the same test, at the place where Guru Nanak was born. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

In the courtyard of a gurdwara at Nankana Sahib stands an old jand tree, a thorny tree of the Punjab plains. Pilgrims stop beside it and bow their heads. It isn't there for its shade. Sikhs remember what was done at that tree on a morning in 1921, at the place tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace. To understand why people bow to a tree, you need the whole story, from the walk in the dark to the fire. Today: Nankana.
screen: `AN OLD JAND TREE IN A COURTYARD.` → `PILGRIMS BOW BESIDE IT.` → `THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the shrine. The gurdwara at Guru Nanak's birthplace was held by a mahant, Narain Das, who ran it as his own. Reformers accused him of misusing its wealth and allowing wrongs within its walls, and they meant to bring it under the Panth's care. Accounts say the mahant knew they were coming and gathered armed men. Second, the walk. A band of reformers led by Bhai Lachhman Singh reached the gurdwara early in the morning. They went in, sat down before the Guru Granth Sahib, and began to recite. Third, the attack. The gates were shut behind them, and the mahant's men opened fire and attacked with blades. Accounts say the reformers had pledged not to resist, and they did not strike back. Many were killed in the hall and the courtyard. Sikh memory holds that Bhai Lachhman Singh, wounded, was tied to the jand tree and burned. That is why pilgrims bow there. Fourth, the old verse that fits. Baba Farid, whose words are in the Guru Granth Sahib at Ang 1378, says that if someone strikes you with their fists, do not strike them in return; kiss their feet and go home. Farid is speaking of the inner life, not of a massacre. But some readers hear his salok beside the story of Nankana, because the reformers lived it at a terrible cost. The news spread across Punjab, and the shrine soon passed into the Panth's care. That's today's line.

Nankana. Nankana Sahib, the place tradition holds as Guru Nanak's birthplace, where peaceful reformers, led by Bhai Lachhman Singh, were killed and did not strike back. Today's word.
Your line: they did not strike back. Today, when you're tempted to hit back, even with words, let one chance pass without answering. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

986.title: The keys, 1921
986.hook: the Sikhs won back the keys of the Golden Temple treasury by peaceful protest
986.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the keys affair, the Chabian da Morcha, as an early victory of the gurdwara reform movement, won by peaceful protest; the toshakhana of the Golden Temple is still kept under the SGPC's management.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nankana, and your line was they did not strike back. Did you let one chance to hit back pass? Today, the same refusal, and this time it wins something. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

A bunch of keys on a ring. They open the toshakhana, the treasury of the Golden Temple, where its precious gifts and offerings are kept. In late 1921, just as the new Sikh committee asks for them, an official acting for the British government takes them into the government's hands. On paper it's a small administrative step. To Sikhs, it's a message: you may pray here, but we still hold the keys. What happens next turns a bunch of keys into a national story. Today: the keys.
screen: `A BUNCH OF KEYS.` → `THE TEMPLE'S TREASURY.` → `TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT.`

segments.voice: First, what the keys meant. The new committee, the SGPC, had begun to manage the Golden Temple. Taking the treasury keys back into government hands said that the British, not the Sangat, still had the last word. Second, the protest. Sikhs answered with meetings, speeches and refusals, all of them peaceful. Leaders were arrested, including Baba Kharak Singh, a respected head of the committee. More volunteers stepped forward and were arrested in their turn. The protest stayed peaceful. Third, the giving way. The protest spread, and the arrests didn't stop it. In the end the government backed down. The prisoners were released, and the keys were handed to Baba Kharak Singh. Accounts say Mahatma Gandhi sent a telegram of congratulation, calling it the first decisive battle for India's freedom won. Fourth, the deeper key. In a salok at Ang 1237 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru is called the key: the mind is a locked room, and only the Guru's key opens it. That verse is about the inner life, not a treasury. But it points at what Sikhs remember about this protest. In their telling, the keys in the government's keeping were never the real power; the Sangat's discipline was. Without striking anyone, the community had won back what was theirs. Gandhi's telegram called it a first battle won, and more were coming. That's today's line.
screen: `WHO HOLDS THE KEYS?` · `MEETINGS, ARRESTS, NO VIOLENCE.` · `THE KEYS HANDED BACK.` · `THE GURU IS THE KEY.` · then, large: `FIRST BATTLE WON.`

Think of something you're working toward that won't come quickly: a change at work, a repair in a family, a habit you're breaking. Breathe in, and feel the key. Breathe out, and decide, quietly, to keep going without forcing it and without giving up. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The keys. The keys of the Golden Temple treasury, taken into government hands and won back by the Sikhs through peaceful protest. Today's word.
Your line: first battle won. Today, take one patient, peaceful step toward the thing you're working on, and count it as a win. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

987.title: Guru ka Bagh, 1922
987.hook: volunteers took police beatings without striking back, and the world saw it
987.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru ka Bagh as one of the peaceful campaigns of the gurdwara reform movement; the gurdwara near Amritsar keeps its memory, and the story is told in histories of the Akali movement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the keys, and your line was first battle won. Did you keep one peaceful resolve? Today ends a week that began with a long memory in London and has turned toward the gurdwaras. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

Dry branches, an axe, and a kitchen fire that needs feeding. In a village outside Amritsar there is a gurdwara called Guru ka Bagh, the Guru's garden, with land around it where acacia trees grow. Sikh volunteers go out to cut wood for the langar, the free kitchen. The custodian who holds the shrine says the land and the trees are his. The police arrest the woodcutters for theft. And then more volunteers keep coming, walking toward the police lines with their hands at their sides.
screen: `WOOD FOR THE LANGAR FIRE.` → `ARRESTED FOR THEFT.` → `MORE VOLUNTEERS KEEP COMING.`

segments.voice: First, the quarrel. Like Nankana and Tarn Taran earlier this week, Guru ka Bagh was in the hands of a mahant, a hereditary custodian, and the reformers said a Guru's shrine belonged to the whole panth. The wood was a small thing. Who owned the garden was not. Second, the jathas. Groups of volunteers set out each day from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, having taken a vow to stay peaceful. At the garden the police met them with heavy sticks and beat them to the ground. Accounts written at the time describe men falling, getting up, and being struck again, without raising a hand. Third, the witness. Charles Freer Andrews, an English clergyman, went to see for himself. He wrote that he watched the blows fall on men who did not strike back, and that the sight brought the crucifixion to his mind. His account was printed and read far beyond Punjab. That is how the world came to see it. Fourth, the root. In the Asa di Var, at Ang 470 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue and all goodness. The volunteers walked to the garden humbly, with no weapon and no curse. But humble did not mean bowed. They walked into the blows on purpose, and when they were knocked down, they got up. That's today's line: beaten, unbowed. And that finishes a week that ran from Udham Singh and Bhagat Singh to the SGPC, Tarn Taran, Nankana and the keys.
screen: `WHO OWNED THE GARDEN?` · `JATHAS VOWED TO STAY PEACEFUL.` · `AN ENGLISH CLERGYMAN WATCHED.` · `SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · then, large: `BEATEN, UNBOWED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes as a witness. Sit, and let your breath slow. C. F. Andrews didn't march. He went, he watched, and he wrote down what he saw. Bring to mind one time you saw someone stand firm while they were treated unfairly: at school, at work, on a street, in the news. Picture it plainly, without adding anything. Breathe in, and remember what they did. Breathe out, and ask: if I told this to one other person, what would I say? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bagh, garden: the Guru's garden near Amritsar, where volunteers walked into police beatings without striking back, and the account of it traveled the world. Today's word.
Your line: beaten, unbowed. Today, refuse to hit back once: if someone pushes you with words, stand where you are and answer without a blow of your own. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

what it means: a question of who owned a Guru's shrine, answered by volunteers who took beatings without striking back.
what a scholar hears: the eyewitness account of C. F. Andrews carried the story far beyond Punjab, which is part of why the campaign mattered.
